summary:
SPHEREx 4D Explorer is an interactive web-based astrophysics platform and REST API designed to transform complex, multi-epoch infrared data from NASA's SPHEREx mission into intuitive 4D visualizations (2D spatial coordinates x Time x Wavelength). Addressing the challenge of hunting for elusive solar system objects ("Planet X"), brown dwarfs, and variable stars across billions of exposures, our tool enables both researchers and citizen scientists to inspect any point in the sky by object name, decimal or sexagesimal coordinates, or direct map click.

For any selected target, the system generates a 54-frame 4D data cube: a 24-epoch temporal timelapse (revealing proper motion, annual parallax, and stellar pulsation) and a 30-channel spectral sweep across 0.75-5.00 um (highlighting H2O, CH4, and PAH features), alongside a 6-Band RGB composite, an Epoch Difference (Delta) image, and a live SVG flux and spectrum chart. This bridges the gap between raw archival FITS files and rapid visual discovery, accelerating citizen science classification across the entire infrared sky.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

SPHEREx 4D Explorer provides a real-time astronomical workstation that processes, aligns, and visualizes multi-band infrared observations:

Interactive Sky Navigation and Reverse Identification: Users can pan, zoom, and click anywhere on the sky using a dual-engine viewport (NOIRLab LegacySurvey / NASA unWISE and CDS Aladin Lite v3) with four spectral filter presets (WISE Mid-IR, 2MASS Near-IR, DSS2 Optical/NIR, and IRIS Thermal Dust). Clicking any coordinate triggers an automated reverse cone search (/api/v1/identify) across our local catalog, the Harvard SIMBAD TAP mirror, and VizieR Hipparcos catalogs to identify the target and generate an astrophysical briefing. Users can also search by object name or NASA sexagesimal (08h55m10.831s, -7d14m42.53s) and decimal coordinates.

Three-Tier Scientific Data Pipeline:

  1. Direct NASA/IPAC IRSA FITS Pipeline: Queries the spherex.artifact and spherex.plane TAP tables, downloads raw FITS cutouts, subtracts zodiacal light (ZODI extension), masks bad pixels via bitmasks (FLAGS extension), extracts exact LVF wavelengths using spectral WCS (key="W"), and reprojects rotated orbital exposures onto a unified 128x128 pixel WCS grid.
  2. Hybrid NASA unWISE 4D Reconstruction: When external TAP servers experience high latency or downtime, the backend seamlessly retrieves real infrared sky cutouts from NASA WISE/unWISE (unwise-neo7, 3.4-4.6 um) and reconstructs a 54-frame 4D cube (24 monthly time epochs + 30 spectral sub-bands from 0.75 to 5.00 um) using seamless Gaussian PSF inpainting, proper motion and parallax modeling, and analytical H2O, CH4, and PAH spectral transmission curves.
  3. Offline Synthetic Fallback: Ensures 100% availability even without internet access.

Multi-Modal Visual Analytics: Every observation returns four synchronized visual outputs:

  1. 4D Animated GIF: Switches between a 24-frame Time-Domain Timelapse and a 30-frame Spectral Sweep with global arcsinh cube normalization and on-frame telemetry stamps.
  2. 6-Band RGB Composite: Stacks SPHEREx bands D1+D2 (Blue), D3+D4 (Green), and D5+D6 (Red).
  3. Epoch Difference Image (Delta I = I_last - I_first): Cancels out stationary background stars into neutral gray while revealing moving objects (like Barnard's Star) as high-contrast black-and-white dipoles.
  4. Live SVG Telemetry Chart: Plots central surface brightness (MJy/sr) across time (light curve) or wavelength (infrared spectrum), displaying zodiacal background levels and pixel quality flags.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Empowering Citizen Science: Raw SPHEREx FITS files have tilted orientations, varying zodiacal backgrounds, and position-dependent wavelengths that are difficult for non-specialists to interpret. Our tool automates WCS alignment, background subtraction, and difference imaging, allowing volunteers to spot moving objects ("Planet X" candidates or brown dwarfs) and variable stars in milliseconds.

Instant Performance and Shareability: A custom SQLite WAL cache with binary zlib compression stores pre-aligned 54-frame 4D cubes, delivering sub-50ms response times. Two-way URL state synchronization (?ra=...&dec=...&sort=...) allows researchers to share or embed specific sky targets directly into external portals.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Astropy (fits, wcs, SkyCoord, Time), Astroquery (ipac.irsa), reproject (reproject_interp), Pillow (Image, ImageDraw), SQLite3 (WAL mode + zlib compression), Pydantic.

Frontend: HTML5, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Tailwind CSS, CDS Aladin Lite v3 API, NOIRLab LegacySurvey Cutout Stream, SVG vector charting, FontAwesome.

External Astronomical Databases: NASA/IPAC IRSA TAP, NOIRLab/NASA unWISE (unwise-neo7), CDS Sesame XML Resolver, Harvard SIMBAD TAP and ASCII Mirrors (simbad.cfa.harvard.edu), VizieR (I/239/hip_main).

How the Project is Creative and Factors Considered

True Axis Decoupling and Global Spectral Normalization: Standard per-frame auto-contrasting cancels out flux differences between spectral bands. We engineered global percentile normalization (global_vmax) with arcsinh stretching across spectral slices so cold Y/T-type brown dwarfs (WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B) genuinely emerge from darkness at 4.5-5.0 um.

Seamless Gaussian PSF Inpainting: Instead of cutting sharp square patches when modeling proper motion on real sky images, we implemented radial Gaussian PSF attenuation matched to local background rings (ring_mask), eliminating visual seams.

Resilience to Infrastructure Outages: Considering real-world server load and outages on astronomical archives (such as CDS Strasbourg and IRSA TAP timeouts), we built a multi-mirror failover architecture and pre-cached all 5 mandatory NASA test targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855-0714, Epsilon Indi Ba+Bb, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) plus 7 deep-sky calibration targets, ensuring zero-downtime operation.
